r: The applied work is building interactive visual representations of large, complex datasets: writing code in modern languages and visualization libraries, structuring data, selecting encodings, and evaluating whether a chart communicates an insight. These map to O*NET activities like Analyzing Data or Information and Interacting With Computers, which observed-usage data identifies as the largest category of model use, and task-exposure research classifies programming among the most positively-exposed activities. AI already generates plotting code and drafts dashboards competently, so the write-the-visualization-yourself rationale is partly eroded even now. The binding consideration is that near-term classroom diffusion and the course's semi-foundational role feeding the DSML capstone hold realized substitution below full automation, and chart design carries a genuine verification burden: misleading encodings and distorted scales are non-obvious failures a trained eye must catch. Rating Medium, exposed applied work but not yet fully displaced at this horizon.

By 2031, AI tools will fluently generate, restyle, and critique interactive visualizations from a dataset and a prompt, handling the encoding selection, layout, and library implementation that occupy most of this course. The semi-foundational role that capped the near term no longer binds at five years, and there is no embodiment, licensure, or hard institutional mandate protecting the material. Task-exposure research places data analysis and programming firmly among exposed activities, and controlled studies show large developer speedups on exactly this kind of code. The instrumental case for a student personally producing visualizations erodes substantially. The residual protection is verification: the jagged-frontier evidence shows users outside the model's competence accept distorted or misleading charts with miscalibrated trust, so a human who understands perceptual encoding retains an oversight role. That is a narrower competence than the course's full content. Rating High.

A decade out, the central case has AI producing sophisticated, audience-tailored visualizations and interactive dashboards on demand, and the applied tasks this course builds toward are largely performed by the model. With no foundational cap, embodiment, or institutional lock binding at this horizon, the instrumental necessity of learning to hand-build visualizations is substantially eroded. The rating is High, hedged by ten-year uncertainty and by the durable residual that visual-analytics judgment, knowing when an automated chart misrepresents the data and choosing what deserves emphasis, retains a verification and curatorial premium held by fewer trained people. Diffusion evidence tempers the pace: adoption of capable tooling lags capability and is uneven across organizations, so realized substitution may trail the frontier. But the direction is clear, and the design-and-analysis work here sits among the most-exposed task categories in the entire evidence base. Rating High.
DSML 2120.d: Students learn to connect the theoretical foundations of data visualization with practical, hands-on design and implementation. They explore data structures and algorithmic approaches for visualization, work with large and complex datasets, and develop interactive visual representations using modern programming languages and visualization tools. Through applied projects, students practice selecting, designing, and evaluating visualizations that effectively communicate data insights in technical and real-world contexts.

r: The applied work is provisioning on-demand cloud infrastructure and standing up data and software services: configuring virtualization, load balancing, redundancy, auto-scaling, security, and serverless functions to run applications, including data-science and ML workloads. These map to O*NET activities such as Interacting With Computers and Making Decisions and Solving Problems. Infrastructure-as-code and configuration are exposed; coding is the largest observed-usage category, and AI assistants already generate deployment scripts, templates, and service configurations competently. The near-term rating is held at Medium by two forces: enterprise diffusion of autonomous cloud tooling is uneven, and the operational verification burden is real. A misconfigured security group or auto-scaling rule causes outages or breaches, failures non-obvious until they bite. The course's semi-foundational role feeding the DSML capstone also limits realized substitution now. AI drafts the configuration; a human who understands the architecture still validates it. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently generate, deploy, and troubleshoot cloud infrastructure from high-level specifications, automating much of the provisioning, scaling, and service-composition work the course teaches. The semi-foundational cap no longer binds at five years, and there is no licensure or embodiment barrier for cloud engineering. Task-exposure research places this configuration-and-coding work among positively-exposed activities, and productivity studies show large speedups on infrastructure and development tasks. The instrumental case for a student manually assembling cloud services erodes substantially. The residual is verification and architecture judgment: the jagged-frontier evidence shows operators who cannot read and audit AI-generated infrastructure accept subtly broken or insecure configurations with miscalibrated trust, and security-critical systems raise the cost of those errors. That oversight competence remains, but it is narrower than the full hands-on curriculum. Rating High, with diffusion as the main pace-limiting uncertainty at this horizon.

A decade out, the central case has AI provisioning, securing, and operating cloud infrastructure largely autonomously from intent-level descriptions, and the applied work this course builds is substantially performed by the model. No foundational, licensure, or embodiment constraint caps the rating at this horizon. The instrumental necessity of learning to hand-configure cloud services is substantially eroded. The rating is High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty and by the residual that security and reliability verification, judging when an automated deployment is unsafe or misarchitected, retains an oversight premium held by fewer specialists. The high error cost of production infrastructure keeps that human check valuable even as routine work automates. Macro-diffusion evidence counsels caution on speed: uneven adoption may leave many organizations short of the frontier. But cloud configuration sits squarely in the most-exposed task band, and the direction of erosion is clear. Rating High.
DSML 3850.d: In this course students learn how to utilize the on- demand delivery of IT resources provided by Cloud Computing to quickly set up software services and applications. Through assignments and projects students create the necessary data and software services to run applications in diverse domains including data science and machine learning. Additional topics covered include virtualization, security, load balancing, redundancy, auto scaling, and serverless computing.

r: The applied work is designing, training, and deploying deep neural-network architectures: implementing models, tuning them, and applying computational techniques to large datasets, plus reasoning about responsible use. These map to O*NET activities like Analyzing Data or Information and Processing Information. ML programming is among the most-exposed tasks in the evidence base; coding is the largest observed-usage category, and AI assistants competently write model code, training loops, and architecture boilerplate. Yet the near-term rating is Medium, not higher, because deep learning carries an acute verification burden. The jagged-frontier evidence is directly on point: model validation, overfitting, data leakage, and distribution shift are non-obvious failures, and users who cannot diagnose them accept confidently wrong models. A human holding this knowledge is required to judge whether a trained network actually works. Near-term diffusion and the semi-foundational capstone role also temper realized substitution. AI writes the model; a trained human validates it. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AutoML and code-generating assistants will design, train, and tune deep networks from high-level specifications, automating much of the implementation this course teaches. The semi-foundational cap lapses beyond the near term, and there is no embodiment or licensure barrier. Task-exposure research places ML programming among the most positively-exposed activities, and GDPval-style evidence shows models approaching expert quality on real technical deliverables. The instrumental case for hand-building architectures erodes substantially. What resists automation is the verification core the course also develops: the jagged frontier means AI-produced models fail in non-obvious ways, biased training data, leaked labels, brittle generalization, and someone must hold the knowledge to catch it. That validation competence is the binding residual constraint, narrower than the full design-and-train curriculum but genuinely durable given the cost of deploying a silently broken model. Rating High, hedged by that persistent verification burden.

A decade out, the central case has AI designing and training performant deep-learning systems largely autonomously, and the model-construction work this course builds is substantially performed by the machine. No foundational, embodiment, or institutional constraint caps the rating at ten years. The instrumental necessity of personally implementing architectures is substantially eroded. The rating is High, hedged more heavily than most by the verification burden intrinsic to machine learning: judging whether a model is valid, unbiased, and robust, the jagged-frontier failure modes, retains an oversight premium held by fewer experts, and the high cost of deploying a wrong model sustains that check. Ten-year uncertainty is genuine, and diffusion evidence suggests realized adoption may trail capability. But ML programming is the single most-exposed task category in the evidence base, and the execution-oriented content of the course is where erosion concentrates. Rating High.
DSML 4220.d: Students learn how deep learning neural networks are able to take advantage of huge volumes of data and abundant computing resources to solve problems traditional machine learning methods can not. Students are also exposed to the basic concepts behind early neural networks and how mathematical and computational techniques can be applied in order to design, train, and utilize modern deep neural network architectures. Ethical implications and responsible usage are also discussed.

r: The applied work is a semester-long synthesis project: scoping a data-science and ML problem in a domain, planning and sequencing phases, building the solution, and communicating progress to internal or external constituents. These map to O*NET activities including Analyzing Data or Information, Organizing, Planning, and Prioritizing Work, and Communicating with people. The technical build draws on the most-exposed task categories, and AI competently assists with the coding and analysis. But the integrative, planning, and stakeholder-facing work is less automatable: negotiating a real client's requirements, sequencing an open-ended project, and communicating trade-offs involve judgment and real-time interpersonal engagement that observed-usage data shows are less represented. The verification burden is also real, since a capstone deliverable is evaluated by constituents against genuine needs. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI accelerates the components, but synthesizing and managing the whole project still requires the student. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will handle more of the capstone's technical components, generating code, running analyses, drafting documentation, and could scaffold project plans and status communications. Yet the course's instrumental core is integration and judgment: framing an ambiguous, domain-specific problem, coordinating with constituents, and owning end-to-end delivery. That synthesis-and-communication work resists full automation more than any single technical task, and the interpersonal, real-time engagement with project stakeholders keeps a human necessary. GDPval evidence shows models approaching but still below expert parity on complete occupational deliverables, which is essentially what a capstone is. The verification burden, constituents judging whether the delivered system meets their real needs, reinforces the human role. The rating holds Medium rather than rising to High: the parts automate faster than the whole, and the integrative project competence remains instrumentally needed across this horizon. Rating Medium.

A decade out, the central case has AI executing most of the technical work and increasingly assisting with project planning and stakeholder communication, so an autonomous or near-autonomous agent could carry much of an end-to-end data-science project. At this horizon the integrative advantage narrows: if models reliably scope, build, and report on projects, the instrumental case for a student personally synthesizing the pieces erodes toward High. No foundational, licensure, or embodiment constraint caps the rating. The residual protection is the real-time constituent relationship and accountability, since someone must own the deliverable and judge whether the automated work actually serves the client, but that is a narrower competence than the full capstone. The rating is High, hedged by substantial ten-year uncertainty about how far autonomous project execution reaches and by diffusion lags that may keep human-led capstones common. Rating High.
DSML 4360.d: This senior-level capstone course reflects a culmination of learning and an opportunity to develop and apply knowledge in the areas of Data Science, Computer Science, Statistics, and Machine Learning to a specific domain. Students identify and engage in semester-long projects that require a synthesis of the knowledge and skills acquired from earlier courses, and that require planning and communication on the phases and progress of the project. Some projects may be solicited from constituents within MSU Denver or externally, and progress evaluated in conjunction with constituent representatives.
